newsitem.title: GERMANY: INTERVIEW - Halle institute sees E. German rebound.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW - Halle institute sees E. German rebound.

text.p: Economic growth in formerly communist east Germany has slowed considerably following a brief surge in the heady period after unification but may soon rebound, a leading economist said on Friday.

Ruediger Pohl, president of the Institute for Economic Research in the eastern city of Halle, said overcapacity in the building industry from years of public aid for construction has led to shrinkage in the sector and has sharply hit overall growth.

The slowdown in the building industry has been one of the main factors dragging on the region's economy, where growth has slid steadily from a high of 9.9 percent in 1994 to a forecast 2.4 percent this year and 2.8 percent next year.
But these figures tell only part of the story, said Pohl, whose institute is one of Germany six leading economic think-tanks and the only one of its stature in the east.
"After 1999 we are again going to see a return to clear growth, not nine percent again, but stronger growth than in western Germany," said Pohl in an interview with Reuters.

"Economic development in the manufacturing industry is continuing and is growing faster than in western Germany. The decline since 1994 is not the beginning of a collapse but rather a second wave of restructuring," said Pohl.

Because eastern Germany's economic output is well below the levels in the west, the slowdown in eastern growth in recent years was of great concern as it meant, in effect, that the gap between the east and west was widening rather than narrowing.

Indeed, the institute predicts manufacturing industry output in the east will expand some 7.4 percent this year and 7.3 next year. The other bright spot is the services sector, which Pohl predicted would grow around six percent this year and next.
Building output in the east is expected to fall 4.5 percent this year and 2.1 percent next year. That compares to growth of 24.5 percent in 1994 and over 30 percent in 1992.
"Capacity in the building sector, when measured on a per-capita basis, is three times as high as in the west. What we are seeing is a normal adjustment of building capacity," he said.

In cities like Leipzig and Halle so many new buildings were erected that offices now stand empty in the downtown area with "For Lease" signs beckoning from the windows. The surplus of available office space led to the collapse of the building boom.

Now, seven years after the Berlin Wall fell paving the way for unification of East and West Germany and unleashing a flood of investment, the former communist region appears to be on the threshhold of the next phase of its reconstruction.

Throughout the country new buildings abound. From small villages to large cities roads have been repaired, sidewalks repaired and modern communications and transport infrastructure rivals that of any western European country.

Where tractors once ploughed the fields of East Germany's vast collective farms, colourful warehouses and shopping centres have sprung up on the outskirts of towns, chock full of western brand names like McDonald's and Ikea.
The east's trademark "Trabbi" car, loathed and endeared alike, is becoming a rare sight on byways now crammed with western models and petrol station franchises from western firms.

While this is clear evidence of progress, it is also just a facade that conceals the deep changes that are still to come, painful changes as east German industry goes through a shake-up that will see thousands of new companies close their doors, Pohl said.
Several years ago it was easy for east German firms to get credit without having to pay interest or start making payments for as long as five years, explained Pohl.

"But now the tab is due and there is going to be a new wave of bankruptcies," he said. "There are a lot of companies that simply are not good and they will disappear. Those that survive will experience new growth."
Pohl said east German industry needed a moderate wage policy, policies that encourage investment and capable management.
